tldr: To solve the problem of robots freezing while waiting for large vision-language-action (VLA) model inference, this framework predicts the next state during action execution to perform speculative inference ahead of time, then selectively repairs only the mismatched parts of the KV cache once actual inputs arrive.
hero_caption: In synchronous inference (a), a full inference stall occurs at every action chunk boundary. In asynchronous inference using initial observations (b), actions suffer from inconsistencies due to outdated inputs. SR-VLA predicts the state at the next boundary for lookahead inference and selectively repairs only differences against real inputs, achieving safe and substantial speedups.
overview:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models handle vision, language, and robot actions within a single model and offer high generalization capability. However, because the models are massive, a single inference pass takes over 100 milliseconds. After executing a multi-step sequence of motions (an action chunk), robots suffer from the painful issue of "control stalls"—coming to a complete stop until the next inference finishes.

An existing countermeasure is asynchronous inference, which starts the next inference pass during current action execution. But this has a major pitfall. Starting inference early means computing future actions based on stale past images, causing significant mismatches with the real environment that has changed due to the robot's own motion. On the other hand, recomputing everything from scratch after real images arrive fails to hide the inference latency.

To address this, the authors devised "SR-VLA". While the robot executes its current action chunk, a lightweight predictor forecasts ahead of time the camera observation and the robot's proprioceptive state at the next decision boundary. A frozen, massive VLA then precomputes a speculative KV cache (intermediate Transformer representations) and an action chunk. When actual sensor inputs arrive at the next boundary, the system checks the differences between predicted and real inputs alongside task conditions. If acceptable, the robot immediately executes the speculative action; if the mismatch is large in critical regions, it selectively repairs only the affected KV cache tokens and regenerates the action.

Experimental results on the LIBERO benchmark demonstrate that SR-VLA achieves a $2.67\times$ query speedup on the representative VLA model $\pi_{0.5}$ and $1.27\times$ on OpenVLA-OFT, all while maintaining competitive task success rates. Furthermore, it shows high resilience to increased inference latency and external perturbations, representing a highly practical breakthrough in real-time control.
contributions: Proposed an input-lookahead mechanism that simultaneously predicts visual observations and proprioceptive state at the next boundary during chunk execution, precomputing a speculative KV cache and action chunk with a frozen VLA.

Developed a two-stage selective KV cache repair mechanism that determines whether to accept precomputations based on task relevance and prediction error upon real input arrival, partially recomputing only the necessary tokens.

Demonstrated speedups of $2.67\times$ on $\pi_{0.5}$ and $1.27\times$ on OpenVLA-OFT on the LIBERO benchmark, maintaining success rates comparable to synchronous baselines even under target-motion perturbations.

sections.heading: How to Fix Robot Stalls: Lookahead Inference and KV Repair
sections.summary: While massive VLA models provide strong task performance, control stalls from heavy inference were inevitable. Conventional approaches failed to reconcile reducing latency with matching the latest environment, but this work overcomes that trade-off by combining input prediction with differential repair.
sections.details:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, which adapt large vision-language models (VLMs) to robot control, are becoming central to general-purpose robotic manipulation. However, inferring massive models from scratch at every decision boundary inevitably incurs substantial latency. For instance, at a 30Hz control frequency, synchronously running state-of-the-art models like $\pi_{0.5}$ or OpenVLA-OFT results in an average control stall of 128 to 135 ms at every boundary, disrupting smooth robot motion.

Prior efforts such as model quantization, pruning, and action chunking (predicting multi-step actions at once) have been explored, yet they do not resolve the underlying synchronous dependency of waiting for the next input before starting inference.

Recently, asynchronous scheduling—beginning the next computation during current chunk execution—has gained attention. However, starting inference early forces the model to plan future actions using stale images, creating a fundamental Latency-Mismatch Trade-off against environmental changes.

The key question here is: how should computation be reused when precomputed results diverge from arriving actual inputs? Unconditional reuse risks safety failures, while full recomputation discards valuable precomputation. SR-VLA elegantly resolves this dilemma by coupling lightweight predicted-input lookahead with selective KV cache repair driven by real inputs.

captions.F1: Comparison of design principles across synchronous inference, conventional asynchronous inference, and SR-VLA. SR-VLA predicts next-boundary inputs and runs VLA lookahead computation during action execution, then repairs differences upon real input arrival to minimize stalls while ensuring accurate control.

sections.heading: VLA Latency Modeling and the Speculative Lookahead Concept
sections.summary: This section formalizes the relationship between action execution time and inference latency, clarifying how much computation can be hidden. It also highlights the key difference between speculative decoding in LLMs and handling future boundary states in robotics.
sections.details:
### II-A VLA Execution Stalls and Metrics
At timestep $t$, a VLA policy takes visual observation $o_t$, language instruction $g$, and robot proprioceptive state (such as joint angles) $p_t$ as inputs, outputting a $K$-step action chunk $A_t = [a_t, \ldots, a_{t+K-1}]$. Let $T_{\mathrm{exec}}$ denote the time the controller spends executing these $K$ steps, and $T_{\mathrm{inf}}$ denote the total processing time required to prepare the next chunk.

Letting $T_{\mathrm{hidden}}$ be the portion of inference time hidden by motion execution, the exposed boundary stall time during which the robot stops is expressed as:
$T_{\mathrm{stall}} = \max(0, T_{\mathrm{inf}} - T_{\mathrm{hidden}})$
In synchronous execution, $T_{\mathrm{hidden}} = 0$ because the robot halts during inference. In asynchronous inference, execution time and inference time can overlap.

In SR-VLA, the computation path splits into a lookahead prediction-and-inference path ($T_{\mathrm{pred}}$) and a post-arrival real input path ($T_{\mathrm{real}}$). Because $T_{\mathrm{pred}}$ runs in the background of action execution $T_{\mathrm{exec}}$, it can be hidden. However, $T_{\mathrm{real}}$—the verification and repair path after real inputs arrive—is necessarily exposed. The core challenge lies in minimizing $T_{\mathrm{real}}$ while effectively hiding $T_{\mathrm{pred}}$.

### II-B Speculative Lookahead and Reusable VLA Internal States
While executing current action chunk $A_t$, the actual observation $o_{t+K}$ at the next decision boundary $t+K$ is not yet available. However, given predicted observation $\hat{o}_{t+K}$ and predicted state $\hat{p}_{t+K}$, the frozen VLA can be executed in advance to construct speculative internal states, such as the KV cache.

Speculative decoding, well-known for accelerating LLMs, also performs precomputation and verification. However, that technique predicts tokens when input text is already available. In contrast, robot control faces the fundamental challenge that future inputs themselves are unobserved. How to verify and repair speculative computation over unobserved future boundaries is the central focus of this work.

captions.F2: Overall execution pipeline of SR-VLA. In the blue and green blocks on the left, next inputs are predicted during motion execution to run VLA lookahead inference (generating speculative KV and actions). In the gray blocks on the right, gating decisions and targeted KV repair occur after real inputs arrive.

sections.heading: SR-VLA Design: Predicting the Future and Repairing the Cache
sections.summary: This section details the overall system architecture, the lightweight action-conditioned input predictor, and the two-stage selective KV cache repair mechanism. It cleverly repairs only necessary tokens via partial forward passes based on prediction errors and task relevance.
sections.details:
### III-A System Overview
The SR-VLA pipeline is clearly separated into lookahead inference during execution and post-arrival verification and repair (Figure F2). While executing current action $A_t$, a trained predictor forecasts image $\hat{o}_{t+K}$ and state $\hat{p}_{t+K}$ at the next boundary. Feeding these through the frozen, massive VLA speculatively generates full-layer KV cache $\hat{\mathcal{K}}_{t+K}$ and action chunk $\hat{A}_{t+K}$. When real inputs arrive, gating logic immediately sends the speculative action to the robot if acceptable; if deviations exist, only affected visual tokens are partially recomputed and repaired.

### III-B Action-Conditioned Next-Boundary Input Prediction
The predictor is an extremely lightweight network with only 10.08M parameters (51.52 GFLOPs at inference). Taking current observation $o_t$, state $p_t$, and executing action chunk $A_t$, it simultaneously predicts next-boundary image and state. Architecturally, action and state are encoded via MLPs into a shared representation; proprioception is predicted with an MLP decoder, and visual observations are predicted with a compact U-Net. Intermediate U-Net features are modulated via FiLM (Feature-wise Linear Modulation) conditioned on the action-state representation, producing image updates that faithfully reflect ongoing arm motion.

The loss function combines a Charbonnier image loss and an MSE state loss: $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pred}} = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{img}} + 0.1 \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prop}}$. In ablation experiments (Table I), naive asynchronous execution without prediction drops closed-loop success rate to 45.2%, whereas introducing this predictor alone restores it to 87.6%.

### III-C Selective KV Cache Repair
To avoid full recomputation once real inputs arrive, SR-VLA introduces two levels of selectivity:
- **Stage 1: Gating whether repair is needed**
  Cosine error $e_i$ between predicted and real visual features is computed and multiplied by task relevance $\rho_i$, derived from attention weights paid by language and action queries during lookahead inference, yielding per-patch risk $r_i = \rho_i e_i$. Repair is triggered only when maximum visual risk $R_{\mathrm{img}}$ or proprioceptive error exceeds a threshold, or when gripper open/close actions occur or consecutive reuse limits are reached.
- **Stage 2: Selecting which KV entries to update**
  When repair is triggered, the update token set $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{upd}}$ is formed by the union of top-$k_e$ error patches (Top-k) and top-$\alpha_r$ ratio risk patches (Top-ratio). Remaining tokens, such as background, directly reuse the speculative KV cache, and only the selected update tokens are routed through layer-wise partial forward passes to repair the KV cache.

sections.heading: Evaluation: Latency Reductions and Perturbation Robustness
sections.summary: SR-VLA is evaluated on the LIBERO manipulation benchmark across two representative VLA models (π0.5 and OpenVLA-OFT). It drastically cuts inference stalls while matching synchronous task success rates, demonstrating robustness against injected computational delays and object perturbations.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
Evaluations were conducted on the robot manipulation benchmark "LIBERO" across four suites: Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long. Base models were $\pi_{0.5}$ (chunk size $K=5$) and OpenVLA-OFT ($K=8$). VLA weights remained completely frozen, and only the lightweight predictor was trained. All experiments ran on NVIDIA A100 GPUs (40GB).

### IV-B Task Quality, Query Latency, and Exposed Stall
Compared to synchronous execution and modern latency-reduction baselines such as VLASH, SR-VLA achieves massive speedups while maintaining high task success rates:
- **$\pi_{0.5}$ backbone**: Compared to the synchronous baseline's 96.4% success rate, SR-VLA achieves 96.9%—matching or exceeding baseline performance—while accelerating query execution by $2.67\times$. Average stall time is sharply reduced from 128.11 ms to 47.95 ms.
- **OpenVLA-OFT backbone**: Achieved a $1.27\times$ speedup over the synchronous baseline and $1.15\times$ over the cache optimization method VLA-Cache.

The repair gate was triggered on average in only 35.98% of queries across the four suites, meaning about 64% of steps safely reused speculative predictions immediately. Even when repair was triggered, the average KV token update ratio across all queries was only 20.48%, keeping computation overhead minimal.

### IV-C Critical-Path Stall and Delay Tolerance
To simulate remote inference environments, deliberate inference delays (+10 ms, +20 ms, +40 ms) were injected. In synchronous execution and VLASH, added delays translated directly into increased robot stalls. In contrast, SR-VLA buffered additional latency within the motion execution window, resulting in a much gentler stall increase (exposed stall grew by only 26.41 ms even under a 40 ms injected delay).

### IV-D Target-Motion Perturbation Robustness
In perturbation experiments, target objects were forcibly moved by 1 to 5 cm during execution. Despite this challenging scenario for speculative lookahead, SR-VLA automatically scaled up repair rates as perturbations increased (triggering repair in 60.26% of steps at 5 cm motion), tenaciously maintaining baseline-comparable success rates. Under these conditions, it preserved a $1.52\times$ – $1.93\times$ query speedup, proving that selective repair functions reliably as a safety valve.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook
sections.summary: SR-VLA demonstrates that combining input lookahead with selective KV repair dramatically curbs control stalls while keeping massive VLAs frozen. It is a practical framework offering exceptional adaptability to inference delays and environmental variations.
sections.details:
This work proposed SR-VLA to significantly alleviate control stalls caused by waiting for inference, the primary bottleneck in real-time VLA control. The core lies in coordinating a lookahead mechanism—which predicts boundary observations and state during motion execution to drive speculative VLA computation—with a two-stage selective KV repair mechanism that efficiently updates only mismatched, task-critical visual tokens after real inputs arrive.

Thorough validation on the LIBERO benchmark shows a $2.67\times$ query speedup on $\pi_{0.5}$ without sacrificing success rates (reducing average stall from 128 ms to 48 ms) and consistent improvements on OpenVLA-OFT. Furthermore, it proved robust in absorbing inference delays from network communication and resilient against sudden object perturbations, matching synchronous robustness.

Requiring no fine-tuning of the base VLA model and acting as a plug-in via an added lightweight 10M-parameter predictor, SR-VLA offers a compelling advantage for future real-robot deployments.

takeaways: Opened a third path—partial repair based on task relevance and prediction error—moving beyond the dilemma of choosing between full recomputation and unconditional reuse in asynchronous VLA control.
High practical utility: requires no fine-tuning of the base VLA, plugging into existing models simply by adding a lightweight 10M-parameter input predictor.
Leverages action execution time as a buffer to absorb computational latency, providing strong resilience against execution jitter in edge devices or remote inference setups.
limitations: Evaluations are limited to the LIBERO simulation environment; full verification under real-robot conditions involving complex sensor noise and hardware communication latency remains future work.
Because the predictor forecasts only one boundary ahead (a few steps), generalization on tasks with very long action chunks or unpredictable, heavy contact dynamics remains unverified.
